slides.title: No parmigiano on seafood pasta.
slides.sub: Yes, really. Even if the waiter is smiling.

slides.heading: Cheese and fish don't mix.
paragraphs: In most of Italy, grating cheese on spaghetti with clams or prawns is seen as a small culinary crime.
Ask for it, and the waiter may suddenly forget how to hear.

slides.heading: Respect the sea.
paragraphs: Seafood has a delicate flavour. A strong, aged cheese like Parmigiano covers it completely.
The Italian philosophy: few ingredients, and each one should taste like itself.

slides.heading: The poor man's parmesan.
paragraphs: Want some crunch? In Southern Italy they sprinkle toasted breadcrumbs — la mollica — on seafood pasta.
Golden, crispy, and 100% approved by every nonna.

slides.heading: Italy is never that simple.
paragraphs: A few regional recipes do mix cheese and fish — and Italians love to argue about them.
But as a guest? Skip the cheese. Your waiter's blood pressure will thank you.

slides.title: Tag the friend who needs to know.
slides.text: Follow for Italian Rule Nº 3 — the one about spaghetti and knives. Brace yourself.

caption:
Italian Rule Nº 2 🍝
No parmigiano on seafood pasta.

Strong cheese hides the delicate taste of the sea — so in most of Italy, it's a firm no. Want crunch? Ask for toasted breadcrumbs, the “poor man's parmesan”.

Team cheese or team no-cheese? Choose carefully. Nonna is reading 👇

—
🇮🇹 Regola italiana n.2: niente formaggio sulla pasta di mare. Siete d'accordo o fate eccezioni?
